Source: The Asiatic Society, Kolkata, G10765; a formatted diplomatic transcript of the Sanskrit manuscript.
Tibetan: D 47.

Those who were intent upon manifesting [the smile] saw the Tathāgata manifesting a smile. Some gods and humans, being intent upon the golden color, saw the Tathāgata as golden-colored;
some saw him as silver-colored, crystal-colored, lapis lazuli-colored, or emerald-colored.
[2r2] The color of an embryo; the color of musāragalva; the color of red pearls; the color of white pearls; blue color; yellow color; red color; pure white color; the color of madder;
the color of the moon; the color of the sun; the color of fire; the color of light; the color of Śakra; the color of Brahmā...
[2r3] Some have the color of vermilion, some the color of snow, some the color of realgar, and some the color of cinnabar; some have the color of water,

some the color of an aśoka flower, the color of a campaka, the color of a sumanā, the color of a vārṣika, the color of a lotus, the color of a kumuda, the color of a puṇḍarīka, the color of Śrī, and the color of Vaiśravaṇa.

Some gods and humans [beheld him] with the color of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king of swans; the color of fresh blue lotuses; the color of Śrīgarbha; the color of ruby; the color of precious gems; the color of sapphire; and the color of the pure splendor of the sky.
Those who have resolute faith in the description of the infinite qualities [of the Buddha] perceive the body of the Tathāgata as endowed with infinite qualities and descriptions.
Thus, Śāntamati, suppose all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system,

as well as the beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were all, by way of conceptual construction, to obtain a human body; and then, suppose one being were to [attain the state of] those very beings...
He should contemplate, resolve upon, and bring forth the physical marks, characteristics, forms, and modes of conduct of the Tathāgata for that many [beings]. And just as that one being [does],
so too should all those beings each individually contemplate, resolve upon, and bring forth the physical marks, characteristics, forms, and modes of conduct of the Tathāgata.
Śāntamati, by this method, the Tathāgata would satisfy the mental inclinations of all those sentient beings such that the mental inclination of one being would not be the same as that of a second;
he would satisfy them according to their respective mental inclinations.

They would perceive the Tathāgata’s complexion, marks, physical form, and deportment; yet therein he would not be diverted from suchness by means of either body or mind. Indeed, it is solely through the effortless excellence of the Tathāgata’s previous conduct and preparatory training that there is the satisfaction of the mental dispositions and intentions of all sentient beings.
Their form, color, marks, configuration, and deportment remain established. Just as, for example, Śāntamati,

when a mirror-disk is perfectly pure, whatever appearance of a form is presented, a reflection exactly like that is seen therein— equal, neither deficient nor excessive— and yet the mirror-disk itself is not...

He intends but does not conceptualize. In the very same way, Śāntamati, the Tathāgata also neither intends nor conceptualizes; yet, without effort, he satisfies the mental inclinations and perceptions of all sentient beings. This, Śāntamati, is the secret of the Tathāgata’s body. Furthermore, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is not...
It is not manifested by the aggregates, nor manifested by the elements,
nor manifested by the sense bases; it is not produced by karma, nor arisen from afflictions, nor arisen from a mother and father.

Born from the great elements of the *kalala* stage, it is not anointed with flesh and blood, nor bound together by bones and sinews, nor dependent upon inhalation, exhalation, and life-force. Furthermore, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is a non-body; it is the Dharma-body, a body that is formless and signless, a body that is without conceptual proliferation and without activity.

To those beings who are intent on the body as having the characteristic of form and who are to be disciplined by the manifestation of a physical form, it appears within the range of their vision; however, to those beings who are intent on the discernment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the nature of form, it does not appear at all, even within the range of the divine eye. In that regard:
Śāntamati, among the beings gathered in a single assembly, some see the body of the Tathāgata while others do not;
some who stand at a distance see it while those standing nearby do not;
some who stand nearby see it while those standing at a distance do not; and some see it by way of mindfulness.
Some see by way of distraction; some do not see by way of distraction. Some see by way of mindfulness;
some see by means of another’s instruction;
some see by means of their own vision; some see by means of the vision of a self; some do not [see] by means of another’s instruction.

Some see while within a dream, but do not see when awakened; some see while awakened, but do not see while in a dream; some see while in meditative absorption (*samāhita*), but do not see when emerged from it;
some see while emerged from absorption, but do not see while in absorption; and some see while in both states.
Some see by way of the aspect of the beautiful, not by way of the aspect of the unbeautiful; some see by way of the aspect of the unbeautiful, not by way of the aspect of the beautiful;
some see with effort, not without effort;
some see without effort, not with effort; some see with exertion, not without exertion.

“Some see it without effort, not through effort; such, Śāntamati, is the body of the Tathāgata. He grants a vision through these and other immeasurable modes. Even those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), whose physical conduct and deportment are perfectly tranquil, whose bodies are composed, and whose bodies are peaceful and self-controlled...”

They too undergo an optical illusion, and they are unable to grasp the measure or the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s body; for, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable because it is manifested as the Dharma-body, which is like space due to its variety of colors. As far as...

Śāntamati, the world is pervaded by the body of the Tathāgata just as it is pervaded by space. Śāntamati, just as space is all-pervasive, even so the body of the Tathāgata is all-pervasive. Śāntamati, just as space is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), even so, Śāntamati...

The body of the Tathāgata is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Just as space is the source of sustenance for all, even so, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is the source of sustenance for all. Just as space, Śāntamati, is changeless and non-conceptual, even so, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is changeless and non-conceptual.
Just as, Śāntamati, space has entered into the manifestation of all forms, even so, Śāntamati,

the body of the Tathāgata has entered into the manifestations of all sentient beings. Just as all manifestations of form are contained within space, even so all manifestations of sentient beings are contained within the body of the Tathāgata.

They are contained within it. Just as all grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees grow within space, even so, Śāntamati, all the roots of merit of all sentient beings grow within the body of the Tathāgata. Just as space, Śāntamati, is neither permanent nor impermanent, and cannot be described by anything at all.
In the same way, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent; it cannot be described by anything.
Śāntamati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas have heads that cannot be seen from above.

[3r6] ...enlightened. I do not perceive anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras, who is capable of looking upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. For what reason? Śāntamati, I recall one [time]...

[3r7] At that time, not long after the Blessed One had attained perfect awakening and was turning the wheel of Dharma while dwelling at Ṛṣipatana in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, from the eastern direction, from the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Campakavarṇa,
from the world-system Arindamā, a bodhisattva named Vegadhārī came to this...

Having come to this Sahā world-system to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him seven times, and stood before the Blessed One.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Vegadhārī: "I shall look back..."

[3r9] Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have upward-pointing heads and bodies that are immeasurable and boundless; what if I were to think that I must seek the measure or the limit of the Tathāgata’s body? Then the Bodhisattva Vegadhārī, having empowered his own body to eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, [stood before] the body of the Tathāgata...
He saw the body of the Tathāgata extending for six million six hundred thousand yojanas.

This thought occurred to him: "I have attained the supernormal knowledges and sport with the bases of psychic power; what if I were to think that I should seek the measure of the Tathāgata’s body even more extensively? Through the power of the Buddha, he did so.

And by the power of his own intelligence, having transcended upward in the direction of space a hundred billion buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system named Padmāvatī. There, a Tathāgata named Padmaśrīrājagarbha currently resides, stays, and maintains himself, and he teaches the Dharma. In that [place], there was a surge...

The bodhisattva Vegadhārī arrived and stood there. Although he remained in that world-system, he was unable to look upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, nor could he perceive the measure or the limit of the Blessed One’s body.
Then, the bodhisattva Vegadhārī approached the Blessed One Padmaśrīrājagarbha.

The Tathāgata approached him; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One, Padmaśrīgarbharāja, the Tathāgata, circumambulated him seven times, and stood before that Blessed One.
Having stood there, he said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how far have I come? The Blessed One replied:
"Noble son, you have come after passing beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in a hundred billion Ganges rivers."

He has arrived at this world-system. He said, "O Blessed One, I have come from afar and yet I am not able—neither to look upon the crown of the head of that Blessed One Śākyamuni, nor to comprehend the measure or the limit of his body. He said, "If you, son of good family, with this very speed and with this very..."

By the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), one might travel for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges toward the upward direction; even having done so, you would still not be able to reach the limit of the body of that Blessed One Śākyamuni. Furthermore, noble son, whatever analogies or illustrations there may be by which the morality (*śīla*) of the Tathāgata...
Whether it be concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation; whether it be the body, speech, or mind;

or whether it be form or the primary marks—it is all these comparisons that misrepresent the Tathāgata, with the single exception of the comparison to space, for as far as space extends, so too does he.
The morality of the Tathāgata is such, his concentration is such, his wisdom is such, his liberation is such,
his knowledge and vision of liberation is such; his body is such, his speech is such, his mind is such, his form is such, and his marks are such.

Therefore it is said: "By means of the immeasurability of space, the immeasurability of the body of the Tathāgata is to be understood. Then, Śāntamati, the Bodhisattva Vegadhārī, having heard this teaching from the presence of that Blessed One, was struck with wonder; he became joyful, elated, uplifted in mind, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness. Toward that Blessed One...

Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him seven times, and vanished from that buddha-field through the power of the Buddha and by his own miraculous strength, he appeared here in this Sahā world-system before the Blessed One Śākyamuni by the mere thought of his mind; he then [bowed] at the feet of the Blessed One.

Having prostrated with his head, circumambulated him, and stood before him with palms joined in reverence, at that moment he spoke these verses: “The man who, regarding the qualities of a Buddha as being like space in nature, desires to reach the further shore, meets with frustration. Even if one were to measure them by hundreds of millions of grains of sand from the Ganges...”

[4r3] How was it? First, I went to the field in order to behold the limit of the Buddha’s body. Having traversed that many fields, I remained in the realm Padmavatī; yet I did not see the end of the Buddhas, nor the measure of their bodies.
In that field, there was indeed a Vināyaka named Śrīgarbha; having understood my intention, he spoke these words:

"Whatever similes people may employ regarding the qualities of a Buddha, they are not commensurate with the Buddha; they will be slandering that Jina. There is but one simile that truly corresponds to the qualities of a Buddha."

The element of space is taught as that for which there is no measure anywhere. As far as this space extends, so far extends the virtue of the Jina; likewise his concentration, wisdom, knowledge, liberation, and the vision of knowledge. Just as space is immeasurable, so indeed is the form of the Buddha. Even the head of the Lord of the World is equal to the element of space.
As far as space pervades, so does the body pervade; as far as the body pervades, so indeed does the light pervade.
As far as the light pervades, so does the speech of the Lord pervade;
as far as the speech of the Guru pervades, so does the mind pervade. Indeed, as far as the mind pervades, so does loving-kindness pervade.

It pervades as far as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) pervades; indeed, as long as knowledge (*jñāna*) pervades, so too does it pervade. And as long as knowledge pervades, so too does the body pervade—so much does one who generates the aspiration for awakening (*bodhi*) pervade through merit. For if the merit arising from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) were to possess form, it would be so vast.

Having filled the realm of space, it would become even greater than that: for as great as is the accumulation of merit acquired by all sentient beings, so great does that of a bodhisattva proceed from the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).

For whatever mass of merit has been proclaimed for a bodhisattva, a much greater merit belongs to one who upholds the true Dharma. Even if all the Buddhas were to manifest with effort for ten million eons, they could not reach its limit.

They would not attain the merit that comes from upholding the true Dharma. The merit derived from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the gathering of the true Dharma does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one who has conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Having gained conviction in emptiness here, one does not abandon the thought of awakening; one upholds the true Dharma—this is the gathering of merits. Having attained this mental state of the Dharma, the highly renowned Bodhisattva [attains] the quality of a Buddha.
He attains this while practicing the conduct of awakening. While these verses were being spoken, millions of buddha-fields trembled;
thousands of millions of gods played tens of millions of musical instruments, and thousands of millions of beings set their minds upon awakening.
Marginal note recording a variant reading: *t* for *kiyat*; *vā* for *pāṭha*. Page 58 of 7.
And having heard Vegadhārin proclaiming the majesty of the Buddha— “For this is indeed an inconceivable,
immeasurable, and unsurpassed state, the secret domain of the Buddhas, the all-seeing self-arisen ones”— he was filled with faith.

This too, Śāntamati, is the secret of the Tathāgata’s body. In that regard, Śāntamati, among the beings assembled in a single congregation, some see the Tathāgata and some do not see him. Those who see him, having become joyful, gaze upon him;
those who do not see him wait in silence. Furthermore, Śāntamati, it is not the case that...

The Tathāgata partakes of food, and sentient beings see the Tathāgata partaking of it. In that regard, Śāntamati, there are deities who attend upon awakening called Ojobalā; they are constantly following behind the Tathāgata, and they receive the Tathāgata’s food with their own food, as do sentient beings.
They see the Tathāgata eating, and each morsel of food taken up by the Tathāgata remains in that very vessel; and those deities, having taken it,
[provide it] to as many beings as are to be disciplined by the Tathāgata and who have previously planted roots of merit, yet [remain there] due to the power of their karmic obstructions.
Having been reborn in those places of birth, they receive no food, drink, or nourishment;
overcome by hunger and weakness, they are presented with the food offered by the Tathāgata.
Having consumed that food, those beings find relief from hunger and thirst, becoming happy and their bodies refreshed.

Those who, with resolute intention, generate the minds set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening— even those who have fallen into the lower realms, such as hungry ghosts or inhabitants of the world of Yama, who are unable to generate the mind for awakening—
that very [act] becomes their cause until they reach final nirvāṇa; therefore, Śāntamati, by this also...
It should be understood in this way by way of a sequence: the Tathāgata does not consume food in that manner;

rather, the Tathāgata has the Dharma as his nourishment. For, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is a Nārāyaṇa-complexion, firm, solid, indestructible, and composed of diamond. Furthermore, Śāntamati, in the body of the Tathāgata there is no stomach for undigested food nor a stomach for digested food.

Neither pus nor blood, nor phlegm nor snot, nor anything impure or unclean is found there. Yet, Śāntamati, behold how the body of the Tathāgata resembles a form of Jāmbūnada gold— impure [is not], without flaw, and irreproachable.

Śāntamati, such is the majesty of the Tathāgata’s body that it is indeed like a diamond in its weight, yet like kācalindika cloth in its softness and pleasant touch; and Śāntamati, there comes a time and an occasion when the gods of great and immense power...

Sons and daughters of noble family, as well as *apsarases*, bowing at the feet of the Tathāgata, experience a touch never before felt; having touched it, they generate the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), and no afflictions arise within them.
Furthermore, Śāntamati, those beings who are dominated by passion (*rāgacarita*) and behold the body of the Tathāgata, simultaneously—

By the mere sight of the body of the Tathāgata, those who perceive it recognize themselves as free from passion; those whose conduct is dominated by hatred, upon seeing it, attain loving-kindness (*maitrī*); those whose conduct is dominated by delusion, upon seeing it, attain the illumination of wisdom (*jñānāvabhāsa*);
and those whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions of the afflictions, upon seeing it, recognize themselves as free from defilements (*vigatakleśa*).

Those who perceive me as one who has passed away become resolved upon renunciation; those who perceive me as immoral become resolved upon morality; those who perceive me with a mind of malice obtain patience; those who perceive me as indolent become resolved upon vigor; those who perceive me as distracted...

Those with distracted minds see it and attain meditative concentration; those with poor wisdom see it and become resolute in wisdom. In brief, noble son, from whatever [perspectives], those beings who have become distant from such pure qualities see the body of the Tathāgata, and by the mere sight of it, they—
In that regard, they become fully stilled in all unwholesome roots and discursive thoughts, and they come to be established in a wholesome mind within the body of the Tathāgata.

And the Tathāgata is without conceptual construction and remains equanimous. Śāntamati, this too is the bodily secret of the Tathāgata: even those emanations (*nirmita*) which the Tathāgata emanates, he does so without effort, without exertion, and without volitional formation; it does not occur to the Tathāgata, "I..."
"I have created, I am creating, I have created, or I shall create"— but rather, as many beings as are to be disciplined by emanations,

so many emanations go to those various places, whether in this world-system or in other hundreds of thousands of incalculable world-systems, for the sake of maturing sentient beings. This too, Śāntamati, is [the nature of things].
Such is the secret of the Tathāgata’s body: even when the Tathāgata emits from his body a radiance of many colors,
various colors, and hundreds of thousands of myriad colors, that radiance pervades the ten directions.

He illuminates as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for the sake of maturing sentient beings, and even that he does with effortlessness, without exertion, and without volitional construction. Śāntamati, this too is the body-secret of the Tathāgata;
this is the purity of the action of the body-secret, which is whatever [penetration] enters therein.

[5r9] Only a mere fraction has been indicated; indeed, one might speak for an eon or even longer, yet it is impossible to reach the limit of the qualities and praises of the Tathāgata’s purity of bodily action.

Furthermore, while this inconceivable exposition on the secrets of the Tathāgata’s body was being taught, the minds of ten thousand living beings were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
And eight thousand bodhisattvas attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*). And the entire assembly...

The assembly scattered divine and human flowers over the Tathāgata and Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas. Then the Blessed One, extending his right hand, which was golden in color, placed it upon the head of Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, and gave his approval, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"

"Lord of the Guhyakas, this well-spoken exposition of the secret of the Tathāgata’s body is approved by the Tathāgata and authorized by him. Thus ends the third chapter, "The Secret of the Tathāgata’s Body," in the Great Vaipulya Sūtra. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Guhyakas, addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
He said this to the Great Being (mahāsattva): "In that regard, Śāntamati, what is the secret of the Tathāgata’s speech? It is the purification of vocal action (*vākkarmapariśuddhi*).
And, Śāntamati, from the night the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until the night [he passes into parinirvāṇa]..."

In this interval, until he attains final nirvāṇa without clinging, not even a single syllable has been uttered by the Tathāgata, nor will he ever speak one. Why is that? Śāntamati, the Tathāgata is indeed perpetually in meditative equipoise; the Tathāgata neither inhales nor exhales, nor does he engage in applied thought or sustained reflection.

And when discursive thought and investigation are absent, no speech issues forth; yet the Tathāgata does not think discursively, does not investigate, does not conceptualize, does not discriminate, does not speak, does not utter, and does not articulate, and yet for sentient beings it occurs thus: "The Tathāgata speaks."

And the Tathāgata, being in ultimate meditative absorption, does not communicate any communication through syllables in any way whatsoever. Yet, for those beings who value syllables, it occurs to them: "The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to us, and we [listen] to the Tathāgata."

We understand the Dharma that has been taught, and therein the Tathāgata is free from conceptual construction and remains equanimous. Furthermore, Śāntamati, no sound issues forth from the Tathāgata’s teeth, lips, palate, tongue, or the opening of his mouth.

And it is heard that this emission of the Tathāgata’s vocal sound issues forth from space, yet sentient beings think, "It issues forth from the very mouth of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Śāntamati, the speech of the Tathāgata issues forth endowed with sixty excellent qualities.

By what sixty aspects? They are as follows: it issues forth as smooth, soft, agreeable, delightful, pure, stainless, radiant, beautiful in color, worth hearing, not harsh, refined, disciplined, not grating, not rough, and well-trained.
It is pleasant to the ear, refreshing to the body, generating elation in the mind, bringing satisfaction to the heart,
producing joy and bliss, free from distress, intelligible, understandable, clear, inspiring love, worthy of being welcomed, and easy to comprehend.

It is intelligible, logical, coherent, and free from the fault of redundancy; it dispels delusion, devours Māra, possesses the force of a lion’s roar, the sound of an elephant, the resonance of a thundercloud, the roar of the ocean, the cry of the lord of nāgas, and the melody of the kinnaras’ song.
It possesses the melodic call of the kalaviṅka bird, is fashioned with the resonance of the voice of Brahmā, and is fashioned with the song of the jīvañjīvaka bird;
it has the sweet sound of the lord of gods, the resonance of a drum, and is neither too high nor too low.
It penetrates all sounds, is free from corrupt speech, is flawless, is not dejected, and is joyful.
It was expansive, friendly, flowing, stirred, sweet, distinct, beautiful to behold,
fulfilling all vocal qualities, satisfying all the sense faculties,
irreproachable, not fickle, not wavering, pleasing to the entire assembly, pacifying passion, and subduing hatred.
It dispels delusion, it swallows Mara, and it is endowed with the excellence of all aspects; such is the speech of the Tathagata, O Śāntamati, which issues forth endowed with these sixty modes.

Furthermore, Śāntamati, the speech of the Tathāgata pervades all world-systems in the ten directions and satisfies the intentions of all sentient beings. Yet, Śāntamati, it does not occur to the Tathāgata:

"I shall [teach] this sūtra, or a verse (geya), or a prophecy (vyākaraṇa), or a stanza (gāthā), or an inspired utterance (udāna), or a causal narrative (nidāna), or a past event (itivṛttaka), or a birth story (jātaka)..."

"Whether I should teach, declare, establish, analyze, explain, clarify, or fully illuminate the Vaipulya, the marvelous Dharma teachings, or the illustrations, the past lives, the legends, the edifying stories, or the narratives; rather, it depends upon the nature of the assembly before the Tathāgata."
Whether it be an assembly of monks, or an assembly of nuns, male novices, or female novices;

or an assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, or mahoragas— whatever the diversity of their faculties and vigor may be, and whatever kind of hearing of the Dharma is required by them, such [is the teaching].

Śāntamati, when they perceive the very same Dharma issuing from the gateway of the Tathāgata’s mouth, that perception of the Dharma causes each of them to set aside their mutual verbal distinctions, and all come to understand their own respective cognitions of the Dharma. This, Śāntamati, is the Tathāgata’s secret of speech.
Furthermore, Śāntamati, the Tathāgata has spoken of the immeasurable conduct of immeasurable sentient beings;

that which is called the eighty-four thousand modes of conduct of sentient beings was taught by the Tathāgata as an introduction for those sentient beings with weak faculties. Nevertheless, it is indeed immeasurable.

[6v2] As for the conduct of beings who act out of passion, Śāntamate, that conduct could be described in a single eon; even longer than that would be the conduct of those who act out of hatred, those who act out of delusion, and those who act with equal proportions of these.

Śāntamati, even if the Tathāgata were to teach the conduct of sentient beings for more than an eon— indeed, if the Tathāgata were to teach the conduct of sentient beings for as long as his lifespan lasts,
remaining for an eon, there would be an end to the Tathāgata’s lifespan, yet there would still be no end to the conduct of sentient beings.

Furthermore, lest there be no opportunity for any other vision of the Dharma, the Tathāgata thus teaches the immeasurable conduct of sentient beings as authoritative, so that sentient beings do not fall into delusion. In this regard, Śāntamati, the speech of the Tathāgata concerns all the conducts of sentient beings.

It issues forth by way of awakening beings to their conduct. This too, Śāntamati, is the Tathāgata’s secret of speech. Furthermore, Śāntamati, those beings who have entered into the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s secret of speech do not perceive the Tathāgata’s speech as issuing from the gateway of his mouth.

They perceive it; however, they indeed perceive it as issuing forth from space. Furthermore, Śāntamati, you might think that beings perceive the voice of the Tathāgata as issuing forth from the gateway of his mouth alone, but this is certainly not how it should be viewed. That...

the Bodhisattva, having made Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, the foremost among them, [accepted the food] from all those sixty goddesses...
That food was taken up by millions of *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and *kinnaras*, and it was consumed by all of them;
yet they did not see one another, and each individual perceived it thus: "This is my food."

[12r4] It was accepted by the Bodhisattva with the thought: "Having partaken of my food, the Bodhisattva will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and may they all likewise awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

They were brought to maturity. Noble son, this is the bodhisattva’s practice called "The Undertaking of Difficult Deeds," a yoga for maturing sentient beings through the acceptance of food. Therein, the bodhisattva, having just bathed and emerged from his body of strength, partook of food and proceeded toward the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

He approached him. As he was approaching, a son of the gods belonging to the earth-realm named Subhūmi addressed all the sons of the gods of the earth-realm and said: "For Dharaṇīndhara is indeed without substance."
Unshakable, free from craving, and having abandoned aversion—that Bodhisattva goes toward the tree, thinking:

"I shall adorn the surface of the earth. And the beings of the earth, entirely delighted, exclaiming "Excellent!", purify this world-system of three thousandfold worlds, scattering flowers, perfuming it with choice incense and fragrances, and sprinkling it with scented waters.
He sprinkles the earth. Indeed, the Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālyadharins, the Vaimānikas, and likewise the Āpsarases, were filled with great joy upon seeing the Bodhisattva and beholding the divine flowers.

And all those world-protectors (*lokapāla*) who reside in the assemblies throughout the four continents, they all cover this entire trichiliocosm here with a net of gold out of devotion to the Jina. And all those Śakras in the world within the trichiliocosm, radiant with light, honor the Bodhisattva, just as he shines among the gods of the Thirty-three (*tridaśa*).

The Vaijayanta palace, adorned in such a way, shines throughout the triple-thousandfold world system. The joyful Suyāma gods completely cover this entire Sahā world-system with a net of beryl for the sake of honoring the Bull among Men. And those Tuṣita gods who are well-contented and perfectly contented—

They adorn [the world] with nets of liberation; they wear necklaces, half-necklaces, and crescent moons, and rain down a shower of coral and pearls. Furthermore, those who are the Sunirmita gods, the kings of gods, fashion a net of bells made of the finest Jāmbūnada gold, making the entire Sahā world beautiful in color and filled with delightful sounds; and all of them—
For those who are joyful indeed, with golden nets— those divine minds which are pure,
of infinite radiance, stainless, and luminous— they, being masters of their own will, fashion this net out of devotion for the one who is skilled in all purposes.

Adorned by nāgas, gandharvas, mahoragas, all the daityas, garuḍas, and kinnaras, as well as by their respective arrays and celestial palaces, the desire realm shines forth. Then, noble son, there was the lord of the trichiliocosm named Vasavartin.

Seeing the Bodhisattva facing toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), Mahābrahmā addressed all the gods belonging to the Brahma realm: "O worthy ones, you should know this: this Bodhisattva, the Great Being, is one who has donned the great armor, who has not relinquished his great vow, and who is firmly armored."
With an untiring mind, he has emerged from all the practices of a bodhisattva;

he has reached the further shore in all the perfections; he has attained mastery in all the bodhisattva stages; he is perfectly pure in all the intentions of a bodhisattva; and he has entered into accordance with the faculties of all sentient beings.
He has thoroughly entered all the secret places of the Tathāgatas; he has completely transcended all the activities of Māra;
he is independent of others regarding all roots of virtue; and he is empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
The great caravan leader who teaches the path for the liberation of all sentient beings;
the destroyer of the entire mandala of Māra; the sole hero in the triple-thousandfold world system;
the gatherer of the medicinal remedies of all dharmas; the great king of physicians, the one who brings about liberation.

The great King of Dharma, bound with the turban of wisdom; the great king of banners who radiates the light of great insight; unstained by the eight worldly dharmas; become like a great lotus; and never forgetting any of the dhāraṇīs of all dharmas.

He has become like the great ocean; free from attraction and aversion, he is immovable and unshakable, having become like Mount Sumeru. He is perfectly stainless, utterly pure, and possesses a mind that is well-disciplined, having become like a great precious gem. He exercises mastery over all phenomena, his mind is pliant, and he has become like Mahābrahmā.
The Bodhisattva approaches the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), desiring to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to overcome the army of Māra,
and for the sake of fulfilling the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
For the purpose of setting in motion the great wheel of Dharma; for the purpose of uttering the great lion’s roar;
for the purpose of satisfying all sentient beings with the gift of Dharma;
for the purpose of purifying the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings; and for the sake of [overcoming] all rival proponents...

For the sake of subduing through the Dharma; for the sake of manifesting the fulfillment of all vows of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and for the sake of attaining mastery and sovereignty over all phenomena. In that regard, O friends, you [should perform] the worship of the Bodhisattva...
[13r2] One should be eager for service; and at that time, he spoke these verses:

The Great Sage, whose being is purified, who is firm in his vows and dharma, and who acts for the benefit of the world including its gods; the God beyond gods, honored by men and gods—he proceeds to the seat of awakening.
For the purpose of subduing Māra together with his hosts, for the purpose of awakening to the wisdom of a Buddha,
for the purpose of fulfilling the Dharma of a Perfectly Awakened One, and for the purpose of setting in motion the wheel of the True Dharma.
Desiring to roar the great lion’s roar, and for the sake of satisfying all embodied beings,
and for the sake of purifying the eye of Dharma in others, the Guide proceeds to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in order to subdue [the adversaries].

In order to fulfill the prior propositions of opposing disputants and to demonstrate the work of a Perfectly Awakened One, the Guide indeed proceeds to the seat of enlightenment. Therefore, all of you, united and harmonious, let us adorn the surface of the earth; behold, O friends, how this triple-thousandfold world system has been adorned!

"Behold the realm of desire! We shall likewise adorn the realm of form, just as the Grandfather [Brahmā] did. With joyful hearts, they said, "Excellent! There, in this Sahā world, they adorned it entirely;
for whatever array was seen in the realm of desire, they displayed it all, surpassing even that worship strewn with flowers.
It was filled with fragrances, strewn with jewels, resounded with the music of instruments, and was both gladdening and worthy of homage.

Indeed, all were filled with joy and acted thus, together with Brahmā and the others, through their various arrays reaching from the Akaniṣṭha heaven down to the lowest realms, and by means of their respective celestial palaces. Furthermore, in the sky above and above, hundreds of millions and sixty crores of divine hosts displayed magnificent ornaments.
Those who adorn the vajrāsana here by sprinkling it all around with perfumed water, scattering it with various flowers and auspicious jewels,
thereby consecrating the surface of the earth— the Bodhi tree thus adorned cannot be fully described by speech.
To proclaim it, they have thus arranged a vast array there as a measure.

And while that son of good family was repeatedly leaning toward awakening, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of a Thousand, addressed all the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-kāyika realm: "O worthy ones, this one..."
Having well-practiced vows and ascetic penances for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, that foremost being,
the Great Man, approached the seat of awakening; there, all the venerable ones—

"The trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system, must be adorned with magnificent arrays. Then, indeed, Mahābrahmā Sahāmpati addressed the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm with these verses: "A being of pure nature, firm in his vows and dharma, seeking the welfare of others, acting for their benefit, and great-souled."
"He is approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree to conquer Māra and his wicked host.

Let us all go together, united and complete; let us adorn this entire earth. For he is a Lord of Dharma in this radiant world, and by honoring him, infinite merit shall be gained. Having heard these supreme words...

Their words, beneficial to the realm of Brahmā, adorned this Sahā world here; they made this Sahā world, consisting of jewels, thoroughly purified and decorated with flowers upon victory banners. By them, tens of millions of parasols were manifested in the sky, as well as arrays of the splendors of the moon and sun, and halls and trees.

Adorned with excellent flowers, they were fashioned by them to resemble the trees of the Nandana grove. That path by which the steadfast one was known (or traversed) here was fashioned for him, measuring seven chariots in width. It was made of jewels, [covered] with gold, and indeed surrounded by seven railings. And the magnificent displays (*vyūha*) that were created there by Śakra—

Indeed, they have been seen before by gods and humans; for just as Śakra’s Vaijayanta [palace], so too do these islands shine when thus adorned. And the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, those of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, and likewise those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, as well as the Akaniṣṭha gods—all of them, endowed with power and speed, adorn [the world].
The most excellent and sublime seats of awakening exist here in the realm of desire, for there are the magnificent displays of the nāgas, asuras, and kinnaras;

all of these were revealed at that very moment when the bodhisattva proceeded to where he was going. Indeed, tens of millions of apsarases came from the four directions to adorn the tree of awakening.
One should sprinkle it from all sides with flowers, perfumes, ointments, and scented waters; thus well-adorned, that Bodhi tree shines like Mount Pāriyātra among the gods of the Thirty-three.
Nor are they able to describe those magnificent arrays created by millions of gods, so exceedingly beautiful. Then,
noble son, as the Bodhisattva was approaching the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), such a radiance issued forth from the two thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet.
By that radiance, the painful sensations of all beings in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama were stilled, and the palace of the nāga king Kālika was filled with a great illumination.
Then the Naga king Kālika, having seen the radiance of the Bodhisattva, was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer;
he addressed his entire harem and retinue in verse: "Proclaim how this golden radiance shines!"
I shine in this abode, and my body is gladdened, as is my very mind.

"I have seen the signs of former Buddhas just as they were seen by me; without doubt, a Great Hero, a Buddha, will appear in the world. Take up fine powders, garlands, perfumes, incense, and ointments;
take up gold, jewels, pearls, conch shells, necklaces, and bracelets. Play the musical instruments and songs!"

And let us raise parasols and banners for Jayasena; we shall perform worship for the Teacher. Whatever beautiful ornaments there are in the Nāgavana grove, we, filled with joy, shall offer them as service to the Sage.
Then indeed, the nāga king Kālika, together with his harem, his wives, his retinue, his assembly, and his sons, [went forth].

Emerging from their own abodes with the sounds of all kinds of flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, musical instruments, cymbals, and songs, they manifested clouds filled with scented water and rained down a shower of fragrant water,
as well as a rain of *nāga*-pearls and *nāga*-flowers.
With great majesty and great splendor of a nāga, she approached the Bodhisattva; having approached,
she together with her retinue performed worship to the Bodhisattva,
bowed her head at his feet, circumambulated him to the right accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and songs, and stood to one side.

Praising him, it is said therein: "By the Supreme Person, having been liberated, this entire field was illuminated; even the three lower realms vanished at that very moment, and the palace of Kāla became suffused with light. For that Nāga king, seeing this, was filled with joy."
The radiance spoke these words: "Without doubt, a Buddha shall appear today, for this radiance is golden-hued. Accompanied by a host of naga maidens, he took up the parasol, the banner, and the robe.

He approached where that Bodhisattva was; having honored him, he was satisfied and full of reverence for him. All the trees, forests, mountains, and clusters of medicinal herbs were filled with flowers of every kind of jewel and gem, and being beautifully adorned, they shone resplendently;
all the trees bent toward the Bodhi tree. All these rivers remained still.
Just as the wind does not cease, so today you shall become a Buddha honored by the three worlds, having overcome Death.

O you of incomparable intelligence, the three lower realms have been eclipsed by the radiance of your splendor—radiance surpassing that of Śakra, Brahmā, the moon, and the rays of the sun—and having been touched by it, they have now become peaceful. That same radiance has followed me today into this forest, which resounds with the emergence of the Buddhas; therefore, may you be pleased.
With a joyful heart, you shall today become worthy; for just as these full jars have come from the realm of the gods to circumambulate you clockwise,

and just as flocks of blue jays in the sky are approaching your right side, so too the entire world, including its gods and humans, stands intent upon honoring you— you shall indeed today be the supreme benefactor of the world.

The path of the virtuous is sought after by wisdom. Indeed, we too have obtained here abundant gains; for I have worshipped the great sage Krakucchanda of great speed, as well as the other, Kanakamuni.
And since I have paid homage today to Kāśyapa, the best of Jinas, and the bull among the Śākyas, I shall never again be separated from the sight of the Munis.

Deprived [of such qualities], he yet aspires for omniscience. O Sage, whose voice is as resonant as the roar of Brahma’s ocean and the lion’s roar, release your speech! Though the earth might pass away, though the best of mountains might move, and though the entire world might cease to exist—for his mind is firmly resolved upon awakening and has arisen through its resolute intention.

Even in ten million aeons, the One Possessing the Ten Powers would certainly not exist; such a possibility does not occur. Then, Śāntamati, the chief queen of the nāga king Kālika, named Suvarṇaprabhāsā, was surrounded and escorted by a great multitude of nāga maidens.
They were attended by women holding various parasols, various garments, various pearl necklaces,
various jewel-encrusted ornaments, various divine and human garlands,
and various incense burners.

They scattered various jewel-flowers over the Bodhisattva as he proceeded, accompanied by the sounding of diverse musical instruments and songs, and they praised him with these verses: "He is undeluded, fearless, unafraid, undismayed,
neither weary nor dejected."

Joyful and invincible, without attachment, without hatred, without delusion, and without greed; dispassionate and liberated—homage to you, O Great Sage! You are the physician who removes the arrow, the disciplined one, the guide, the excellent healer, and the deliverer of people from their sufferings.
Having recognized those who are without shelter, without protection, and without an island, you have arisen as a shelter and a protection in the three worlds.

Just as the hosts of gods are pleased and overjoyed, raining down a great rain of flowers from the sky and casting great clouds of garments, O Great Sage, O Victor, may you bring joy to the people; please come!
O fearless one, sit upon the king of drums! Shatter the army of Māra and cut through the web of afflictions!
Awaken to the supreme, peaceful, and excellent enlightenment, just as it was awakened to by the Victors of the past—for the sake of which you have practiced for many millions of eons.

Difficult deeds have been performed for the sake of liberating all beings. Those hopes are fulfilled; this is the time to reach it. Sit upon the king of trees and touch supreme enlightenment! Then, O son of good family, the Bodhisattva, having emerged from the abode of Kālika, the Nāga king, proceeded toward the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
As he was approaching, on his right side there was a grass-cutter named Svastika who was gathering grass.

Seeing the Bodhisattva facing toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), and being urged by the deities, he [offered] grass that was soft, delicate, lovely, charming, and like the color of a peacock’s neck.
Taking a bundle of fragrant grass that was scented, soft to the touch like kācalindika cloth, and curled to the right in a clockwise direction, he approached the Bodhisattva; having approached,
he gave the bundle of grass to the Bodhisattva and, with a resolute intention, directed his mind toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, noble son, you might think that Svastika the grass-cutter has now for the first time and for the last time generated the thought of awakening and is offering grass.
But it should not be viewed in this way. Why? Because this was the former vow of Svastika."

"Just as for the grass-cutter, may I likewise spread seats upon the seat of awakening for all the bodhisattvas of this Fortunate Aeon. For what reason? I recall, noble son, that in the past, ninety-one aeons ago from this present Fortunate Aeon, there was a Tathāgata named Vipaśyin.
The Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world,
the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. In his teaching, there was a full thousand of monks.

He practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He was prophesied by that Blessed One, saying: "In the Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), you shall all fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. At that time, in that very assembly, there was a householder named Mati who had gathered there; he sat down among them.

Having heard the prophecy of the bodhisattvas regarding their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he generated the mind set on awakening and made this vow: "May I indeed perform the preparation of the lion-thrones for those Tathāgatas of the Fortunate Aeon as they approach the seat of awakening."

Furthermore, noble son, do you have any doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation that at that time, on that occasion, there was another householder named Matimān? Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Why is that? Because at that time, on that occasion, this very Svastika the cart-driver was the one named Matimān.
He was a householder. Therefore, noble son, by this means as well as that, it should be understood in this way:
such was his former vow. [Regarding] Svastika the grass-cutter, from whom did he [receive it]?
Page 23, 58.

To some he will give a bundle of grass; to others he will offer lion-thrones arrayed with jewels, according to the needs of beings who are liberated and whose faculties are fully matured. Then, O son of good family, as he approaches the seat of awakening, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the deity of the Bodhi tree—

Then, together with thousands of goddesses from the ten directions, each holding baskets of flowers, they approached the Bodhisattva; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva and scattered upon him the flowers, perfumes, powders, and ointments that they had brought. Āḥ!

And with these verses he praised him: Homage to you, the Great Soul—fearless, steadfast, peaceful, self-controlled, joyful, contented, radiant, delightful, blameless, liberated from faults, the Teacher! Homage to you, the sole protector for this helpless people burning in great suffering; you alone are the source of happiness.
O giver of this [teaching], the great king of physicians for the world to eliminate the disease of afflictions—O Yaśasvin, homage to you! We are serene and overjoyed, just as the hosts of gods are;
and just as a divine rain of flowers has fallen, so shall you surely attain the noble, supreme enlightenment after having conquered the enemy Smara with loving-kindness.

Approach the king of trees and sit upon this seat; having utterly conquered Māra, dispel all darkness and awaken to the peaceful, supreme, and foremost enlightenment, just as it was awakened to by those former lords of sages. Just as your purity...
"May that which was accomplished through difficult austerities for the sake of liberating the world endure for ten million eons; today, O Great Seer, your supreme aspiration is fulfilled.
Sit upon this king of trees and awaken to enlightenment! Then, O son of good family, the Bodhisattva—

Taking a bundle of grass, he approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). Having arrived, he himself spread out a mat of grass at the foot of the Bodhi tree, paid homage to the Bodhi tree, and circumambulated it seven times.
Immediately after the mat of grass had been prepared by the Bodhisattva, O son of good family, then by them—

Moreover, eighty-four thousand sons of the gods had prepared eighty-four thousand lion-thrones for the Bodhisattva— variegated, beautiful to behold, lofty, and elevated, inlaid with every kind of jewel, adorned with jeweled railings, and covered with jeweled nets.

They were covered with networks of small bells, hung with strings of pearls, and adorned with many hundreds of thousands of fine fabrics. There, noble son, the Bodhisattvas sat upon all those lion-thrones.

The self was manifested, yet those sons of the gods did not see one another, nor did they recognize one another. Each son of the gods perceived it thus: "The Bodhisattva is seated upon my lion throne;
having sat upon my lion throne, he will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
By that very joy and gladness, they became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, noble son, as soon as the Bodhisattva had sat down upon that lion throne,
there issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows a light called "Exhortation to Māra.
By that light, a hundred *koṭīs* of Māras in the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were touched.

Remaining in their own abodes, they stood with the hair on their bodies bristling with joy; yet they perceived their respective Māra-palaces as being ablaze. Their splendor was eclipsed, and this thought occurred to them: "What indeed could be the cause here? What is the condition by which these palaces..."

They appeared dimmed; looking out, they saw that the Bodhisattva had indeed sat down at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and was about to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Page 24, 58.

[The Bodhisattva] sat upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). Then those wicked Māras vanished from their respective abodes. And each individual Māra appeared with immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yakṣas, possessing various colors, various costumes, and various forms.
Surrounded by various mounts, various garments, various heads, various weapons, and various banners,
each one uttered diverse lamentations with great power of Māra and great magical might of Māra.
Māra, having surrounded himself with an assembly of Māras twenty thousand yojanas in width and eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth, approached the foot of the Bodhi tree.
As soon as those members of Māra’s assembly had approached, O son of good family, at that very moment—

A sound such as that—pleasing to the mind, worth hearing, yet unbearable—was uttered: "Strike! Crush! Rend! Shatter! Seize! Kill! Slay! If those noble sons who were not free from passion heard that sound, hot blood would gush from their mouths and they would die.
If that son of good family, the bodhisattva, had not caused that sound to vanish— whether it were the approach of execution or the mere suffering of death— then,
being overwhelmed by great compassion, the bodhisattva caused that sound to vanish so that beings would not suffer harm.
Thus it is said. This too, noble son, is the domain of a bodhisattva’s skill in means.
And having heard such a sound, noble son, not even a single hair on the bodhisattva’s body stood on end.
Why is that? Because he has thoroughly understood all sounds to be like echoes. He approached, noble son.
Having perceived Māra’s assembly, the deities who attend upon the Bodhi tree dissuaded the Evil Māras from their purpose by means of sixteen modes of dissuasion: "Enough, O Evil Ones!
What is the use of such efforts at obstruction, which are so difficult to overcome? Why is that?"
Today you evildoers shall be slain by the Bodhisattva, like a wicked wrestler by a great wrestler;
today you evildoers shall be defeated by the Bodhisattva, like a hostile army by a great hero; today you evildoers shall be overcome by the Bodhisattva.
Just as fireflies are eclipsed by the orb of the moon, today you, O evil ones, shall be cast down;

just as a handful of chaff is scattered by the Bodhisattva like the wind, today you, O evil ones, shall be made to fall; and just as a great śāla tree is uprooted by the Bodhisattva, today you, O evil ones, shall be terrified.

Today you wicked ones shall be exhausted by the Bodhisattva, just as a herd of deer is by a great lion. Today you wicked ones shall perish by the Bodhisattva, just as water standing in a cow’s footprint is by the heat of the sun. [By the Bodhisattva], like an enemy city...

"By the Great King! Today you evildoers have been observed by the Bodhisattva like a rogue caught while escaping from execution. Today you evildoers shall be confounded by the Bodhisattva, like a merchant whose abundant provisions of food are consumed by a fire."

Today you, the wicked ones, shall wither away; by the Bodhisattva, the King of Unrighteousness has been ousted from his kingdom. Today you, the wicked ones, shall be consumed; by the Bodhisattva, like an old crane whose wings have been plucked. Today you, the wicked ones, shall be destroyed; by the Bodhisattva, like those who have entered a wilderness forest.
Like those whose provisions for the journey are exhausted, you who are most wicked shall today be swept away. Like Bodhisattvas caught in the middle of the ocean with their ship wrecked, you today—

"O evil ones, you shall wither away! By the Bodhisattva, you evil ones shall be scattered today like grass and forest plants by the time of the conflagration at the end of an eon; by the Bodhisattva, you shall be shattered like stones by a great thunderbolt. Thus, O son of good family, did the deities who attend the Bodhi tree address those Māras, the evil ones.

He exhorted them with the sixteenfold method of dispassion, yet those wicked Māras did not turn back. Then, noble son, the Bodhisattva— [due to] his generosity, self-control, restraint, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons—

Having extended his right arm— golden-colored, soft, tender, delicate, and well-formed, which had been refined by the cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, tranquility, insight, and the liberation through the destruction of ignorance— he raised it as far as his head.

Having rubbed his entire body, with a resolute intention directed toward the liberation of all sentient beings, impelled by great compassion, he brought to mind and remained mindful and clearly aware of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout all the world-systems below the great earth.

[17r5] ...he struck her with his hand. As soon as she was struck by the Bodhisattva, O son of good family, the great earth then shook in six ways at that moment: it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely; it quaked, it quaked violently, it quaked intensely; it shuddered, it shuddered violently...

It shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely; it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely; it rattled, it rattled violently, it rattled intensely; it roared, it roared violently, it roared intensely. It sank in the eastern direction and rose up in the western direction;
it sank in the western direction and rose up in the east.

The eastern direction rose up, and the southern direction sank down; the northern direction rose up, and the southern direction sank down; the southern direction rose up, and the western direction sank down;
from the center it rose up, and from the periphery it sank down; from the center it rose up, and from the periphery it sank down.

[17r8] He rejoiced. For in this way, O son of good family, at that very moment, there appeared in the world a great earthquake with six modes and eighteen great omens. And the wicked Māras heard the sound: "Great shouting, crying out, seizing, striking, and killing!"

They listened. From the sky above the assembly of Māra, through the power of the Bodhisattva, they heard this kind of sound: "Go for refuge indeed to this seer endowed with virtue; for he is the giver of fearlessness and the protector of all embodied beings. And having heard that sound, O son of good family, the eighty-fold assembly of Māra...

Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *tiyakṣaka*s fell face down upon the surface of the earth and uttered these words: "Save us! Furthermore, the remaining wicked Māras, together with their military hosts, desired to flee but were unable to do so; out of compassion for them—

[17v3] Starting from that moment, a radiance was emitted from the body of the Bodhisattva by which all their fears were dispelled, and they each returned to their own respective abodes. Furthermore, noble son,
while this display of the Bodhisattva’s prowess in subduing Māra was being shown, the assembly of Māra was rendered invisible.
[17v4] Then, the minds of many thousands of *koṭī-niyuta-śata-sahasra* of yakṣas were set upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, the minds of nine other hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta-śata-sahasra* of living beings were set upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment. And the minds of eighty-four thousand sons of gods (*devaputra*) who had previously cultivated [the roots of virtue] were set upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

Knowledge..."

O Pure Being, your conduct is purified; you are renowned throughout the three worlds and filled with a multitude of royal virtues. You are more pure than the moon and utterly stainless; you possess a radiance that surpasses the sun and is most brilliant.

O foremost in splendor, O you whose voice surpasses that of Brahmā, O sweet-toned one, O Brahma-voice! I pay homage today to the Three Jewels, which are stainless and possess a golden radiance. You manifest a body, yet you are not bound by a body; you speak words, yet there is no cessation to your speech.

Folio 34, page 58 [23v5]: A Kalpa. You speak the Dharma, yet for you there is no "I" in that; it is truly the Dharma which effects the liberation of beings, yet there is no perception of a "being. It would never be possible for all the worlds together to do you any favor.

Free from the afflictions of household life—those who, having followed you, instruct others, and whose essence consists in the realization of reality as it has been definitively established elsewhere.
The seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition," is concluded. Then, indeed, Vajrapāṇi...

The Lord of the Guhyakas and that entire assembly covered the Blessed One with those garlands of variegated jewel-flowers as they were offered. Immediately upon being cast down, at that very moment, this—
The trichiliocosm, adorned with various flower garlands,
appeared as a well-arranged expanse laid out like a checkerboard.

[23v8] This was through the power of the Buddha. Then the Bodhisattva Śāntamati said this to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas: "Lord of the Guhyakas, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgata. He replied: "I have been prophesied, noble son, by means of the prophecy concerning the nature of dreams. He asked: "For the sake of attaining what?"

“You have been prophesied. He said, “Noble son, the attainment of a prophecy is for the sake of non-attainment. He asked, “What is it that one does not attain? He replied, “One does not attain sentient beings, life, or a person; one does not attain nourishment. One does not attain the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, up to and including roots of merit that are with fault, without fault, or with outflows.”

[One] does not obtain the untainted, the mundane, the supramundane, the conditioned, the unconditioned, affliction, purification, saṃsāra, or nirvāṇa. He asked: "If one does not obtain them, what is explained here? He replied: "The knowledge that follows that non-apprehension is what is explained. He asked: "But what, moreover..."
He said: "Knowledge is manifested as non-dual. If duality were manifested, there would be no prophecy;
because knowledge is manifested as non-dual, therefore Bodhisattvas are prophesied precisely by means of the prophecy of non-duality. He asked: "If not..."

Who prophesies the knowledge manifested as non-duality, or who is prophesied? He said: "He who prophesies or who is prophesied—those have attained equanimity; they possess the limit of non-duality. He said: "Lord of Guhyakas, what is the prophecy regarding that limit of non-duality? He said: "That very limit of non-duality is itself the limit of that [limit]; it is precisely the limit of that."
[The question on] prophecy. He asked: "In what limit (koṭi) established does prophecy occur? He replied:

"Prophecy occurs for one established in the limit of the self (ātma-koṭi); prophecy occurs for one established in the limit of sentient beings (sattva-koṭi), or established in the limit of a living being (jīva) or a person (pudgala). He asked: "To whom does the station of the limit of the self belong? He replied: "The station of the limit of the self..."

"The limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation. He said: "The limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation. [24r6] He said: "The limit of ignorance, becoming, and craving. He said: "The limit of ignorance, becoming, and craving—of what is it the limit? He said: "The limit of absolute non-arising and non-origination. He said: "Of that which has not arisen, what is the limit?"
He said: "The locus of informative intimation. He said: "What does informative intimation inform? He said:
"If, while informing, it were not non-informative (avijñapti), [what would happen? He said: "What does it not inform? He said: "All informative intimation does not inform. He said:
"If it does not designate (prajñapayati), how does it command (ājñāpayati)? He said: "If it were to command, it would not inform; because..."

He does not inform. Therefore, he commands. He asks: "How is it that one has been commanded? He says: "When one does not accept the communication. He asks: "How does one not accept the communication? He says: "When one does not pursue the literal expression. He asks: "When do you pursue it? He says: "How do you pursue it?"

He said: "When one does not see the object. He asked: "How does one not see the object? He replied: "When one is neither in the object nor desirous of the object. He asked: "When one is neither by means of the object nor desirous of the non-object, who then is it that is not desirous?"

He said: "When one is neither desirous of gain nor desirous of non-gain, then one is desirous of the Dharma. He asked: "If one is desirous of the Dharma, is one not indeed desirous of something? He replied: "Noble son, one who is desirous of the Dharma is not desirous of anything at all. Therefore, whatever one is desirous of is non-Dharma; it is not the Dharma. He asked:

"What, then, is non-dharma? He replied: "That wherein even the word 'dharma' is not perceived. He asked: "What dharma is there in that which even the word 'dharma' is not perceived? He replied: "O son of good family, that very thing is non-dharma wherein syllables do not exist."
[24v2] They practice accordingly. Therefore it is said: "All phenomena are ineffable; they are without sound and beyond utterance.
Noble son, he who thinks "I am sinking" or "I am sinking away" is one who sinks. And for him who sinks, there is neither Dharma nor Vinaya. He said:
"O Lord of Guhyakas, surely the Tathāgata does not sink—he who sinks away from the Dharma?"

[24v3] Thus it was said. He replied: "But, noble son, have I not previously declared that not even a single syllable was uttered or spoken by the Tathāgata? He asked: "What fault is there in uttering one? What fault is there in uttering verbal action?
He replied: "What fault is there in verbal action? He replied: "The fault of being overwhelmed by reflection on syllables."

[24v4] He asked: "What, then, is faultlessness? He replied: "That which is not uttered, not proclaimed, and for which there is no communication whatsoever, whether manifest (*vijñapti*) or unmanifest (*avijñapti*), by which one makes oneself known or another—this is faultless. He asked: "What is the root of fault? He replied: "Grasping (*udgraha*) is the root of fault. He asked: "What is the root of grasping? He replied: "..."

[He] does not take craving as an object of focus. He said: "One does not take the latent tendency of craving as an object of focus. Therefore, noble son, it is for the sake of abandoning the object of focus that is craving that the Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata. Now, while this exposition was being delivered by Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas, the minds of five hundred monks [were liberated].

Having released [the two], both of those beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, his resolve fulfilled, having been prophesied, attained consolation, and was satisfied and elated.

With a joyful mind, delighted and filled with gladness and happiness, he said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One come to our royal capital, Abhayā, and stay for seven nights in our Guhyaka abode together with the Bodhisattvas and the great Śrāvakas, out of compassion for us. Then...

Having heard it, it will for a long time lead to their welfare, benefit, happiness, and well-being;

and thereafter, those with angry and wicked minds will desist from them. Furthermore, O Blessed One, it will also for a long time lead to the welfare, benefit, happiness, and well-being of the retinues of the four Great Kings. [The Blessed One] consented.

The Blessed One, out of compassion for Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the guhyakas, remained in silence for seven nights in the palace of the lord of the guhyakas within the royal capital of Āḍakavatī, together with the bodhisattvas and the great śrāvakas.

58] [25r2] For the sake of increasing the roots of virtue of immeasurable sentient beings, and for the sake of fulfilling the intention of Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas. Then, indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas...

Having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, he was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One,

In the eastern direction from this world-system, having passed beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,

"I shall measure out mandalas and pavilions for the purpose of making offerings to the Blessed One. Then, at that moment, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, entered the meditative absorption named Mahāvyūharāja. As soon as Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, had entered the Mahāvyūharāja...

Then, at that moment, by means of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*), a mandala array appeared within the center of the Blessed One’s royal capital, exactly like the arrays found in that world-system called Ānandaguṇaratnavyūha;
it was vast and extensive, measuring sixty-four *yojanas* in length from east to west.

And it is thirty-two *yojanas* in extent from south to north, with a ground surface made of blue *vaiḍūrya*, and surrounded by walls made of *indranīla* jewels, inlaid at their edges with all kinds of gems.

It was strewn with divine jewels and flowers, variegated, beautiful, and delightful; it brought refreshment to the body and joy to the mind, a collection of infinite virtues beyond measure or description. And within that circular hall, many hundreds of thousands of lion-thrones appeared, with feet made of jewels.
[25v4] They were strewn with [jewels], surrounded by jeweled railings, adorned with arrays of jewel-lotuses, covered with nets of pearls, laid out in a checkerboard pattern,

arrays such as had never been seen or heard of before, and which did not exist even in many world-systems.

He prepared food refined with a hundred flavors; he established ten thousand lion-thrones not fixed by means of *dhāraṇīs*; and each individual lion-throne he covered in the sky with a jewel-canopy endowed with the excellence of all aspects. Then, indeed, Vajrapāṇi...
O Lord of the Guhyakas,
[he] beheld these very arrays of mandalas and arrays of lion-thrones of such a form.
Having measured it out, being mindful and clearly comprehending, he then emerged from meditative concentration; that very night,
he prepared an abundant and exquisite array of various flavors— a meal worthy of offering to the Tathāgata through the purity of the Bodhisattva’s resolute intention.
At the end of that very night, he addressed the Four Great Kings: "Friends,
you should know that the Blessed One has been invited by me to my own Guhyaka palace, together with the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and Great Śrāvakas, and he has accepted."
Seeing him preceded by a host of gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmā-parivāra, they were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted,
and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, for the purpose of making an offering to the Blessed One.
With divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, pāriyātraka flowers,

mañjūṣaka flowers, sthāla flowers, mahāsthāla flowers, roca flowers, mahāroca flowers, mahācakra flowers, fragrant-scented flowers, hundred-petaled flowers, thousand-petaled flowers, kokanada flowers, jyotiḥprabha flowers, jyotīrasa flowers, samantagandha flowers, nityagandha flowers, and sadāpuṣpita flowers.

They scattered these and other delightful flowers over the Blessed One; they raised up parasols, banners, and flags, and played hundreds of thousands of musical instruments. Then, indeed, the Blessed One was amidst such an array as this, with rains of flowers falling.
As showers of perfumes, garlands, ointments, and powders fell, as musical instruments were played in concert,
and as hundreds of celestial maidens sang his praises,
he arrived at the royal capital of Āḍagavatī in a single moment, an instant, and a brief hour, before Vaiśravaṇa.
The assembly hall of the Great King was established; together with the Bodhisattvas,
Mahāsattvas, and Mahāśrāvakas, as soon as the Blessed One had taken his place upon the surface of the earth, at that very moment,
a great earthquake occurred.

[It was] real; it was soft, subtle, and non-harming to sentient beings. Then indeed, the four great kings, having learned that [the Blessed One] had arrived at the royal capital, hurried very quickly, accompanied by their harems, their kinsmen, and their retinues, [carrying] flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and powders.

Taking it with them, they approached the place where the Blessed One was; having arrived, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and, having performed worship of the Blessed One with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments as they had brought them, they stood to one side. He engaged them in a delightful discourse; thereupon,
