They generated the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Then, indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas,
together with his harem, his own kinsmen and retinue, and his assembly, accompanied by a retinue of infinite arrays of virtues—
With all kinds of flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, incense, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, musical instruments, cymbals, drums,
and the sounding of songs and music, he went toward the assembly hall of the great king Vaiśravaṇa.

Having approached the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and performed worship to the Blessed One with the flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments,
powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags that he had brought along, according to the prescribed rites.

Having paid homage to the Blessed One with the sounding of musical instruments and songs, he entered his own circular pavilion. Together with the community of monks, the Blessed One sat down in that circular pavilion upon the seat as it had been prepared.

There, upon his own lion throne—which was not fixed to the surface of the earth and was endowed with the excellence of all aspects—those bodhisattvas and those great śrāvakas sat down according to their respective seats, as did the entire assembly. Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas, said this to that assembly of gods: "May the Blessed Ones come forth! and he performed [the welcoming rites].

[26v5] ...the service and worship of the Tathāgata has been described by the Tathāgata himself. In that regard, those who rejoice and perform acts of assistance—their gift is not deficient; they too are partakers of merit. Therefore, friends, you should accept this basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing. Then indeed, they...

Having seen the arrays of mandalas and the arrays of lion-thrones belonging to the sons of the gods, they were struck with wonder and uttered this inspired exclamation: "Whose power is this? Is it that of the Tathāgata, or rather of the Lord of the Guhyakas?"

They heard a sound from the intermediate space. This was the empowerment of the Lord of Guhyakas: "O worthy ones, in the eastern direction, beyond as many buddha-fields from this buddha-field as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,"

There is a world-system named Anekaguṇaratnavyuha; there, a Tathāgata named Vyūharāja teaches the Dharma. There, Guhyādhipati beheld such an array as this; that very array was established by Guhyakādhipati within this mandala-circle. Immediately upon the Blessed One’s sitting down there—

On the lion throne. Now, at that time, as many yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, gandharvas, guhyakas, and mahoragas as resided in the royal capital of Bhagavatī all approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One. Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, addressed the four great kings and the entire assembly: "Come, all of you, together and in harmony."
"Having become so,

we shall present the Blessed One with food prepared according to our vow. Then indeed Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, together with his harem, his kinsmen, his assembly, his sons, his forces, and his retinue—

With his own hands, having prepared and served it with respect, he satisfied and regaled the Tathāgata, along with the assembly of Bodhisattvas, the assembly of monks, and the community of bhikṣus, with abundant, exquisite food of many hundreds of flavors—food purified by the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of a Bodhisattva and worthy of offering to a Tathāgata. Having satisfied them, he regaled them. Having regaled them...

Perceiving that the Blessed One had accepted the bowl and was sitting with hands washed, he sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. And those yakṣas and rākṣasas who dwelt in the royal capital of Bhagavatī also remained there.
Having assembled, they stood gazing at the face of the Blessed One, with palms joined in reverence, paying homage. Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, made this request to the Blessed One:

For the sake of teaching the Dharma: May the Blessed One teach such an entry into the method of the Dharma that sentient beings who have not yet generated the mind of awakening may generate the minds directed toward awakening, and [attain] the state of non-retrogression.

They should remain steadfast. And for this assembly of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, gandharvas, guhyakas, and mahoragas, it shall be for their long-term welfare, benefit, happiness, and security; and they shall especially rise toward excellence and distinction. And...

They would become partakers of the light. When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, and that entire assembly: "Therefore, friends, listen well, attend thoroughly, and take to heart this method of the Dharma."

“I shall explain the entrance into which sons and daughters of good family, having entered, will exert themselves in the yoga of progressing toward distinction and will not be subject to decline. “Excellent, Blessed One! said Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, and that entire assembly addressed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One listened to them and said this to them: "In this regard, friends, a son of good family or a daughter of good family,
having generated the mind set on unsurpassed perfect enlightenment with a resolute intention, becomes faithful."

Abounding in serene faith, desiring the sight of the noble ones, and desiring to hear the true Dharma; free from stinginess, liberated in generosity, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, a patron of sacrifices, devoted to the distribution of gifts through acts of giving, and taking pleasure in sharing.

With an unobstructed mind and a compassionate heart, he has faith in and conceives of the ripening of karma; he understands it, becoming free from doubt, free from hesitation, and free from uncertainty. Having realized that there is no loss of the fruit of black and white karmic actions, he does not commit what ought not to be done, even for the sake of his life.

He abstains from taking life; he abstains from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, from frivolous chatter, from covetousness, from ill will, and from wrong view. He [practices] these ten paths of wholesome action.

At the outset, he does not turn toward or take up the ten unwholesome paths of action. He should associate with those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have gone rightly, who have entered upon the right path, who are virtuous, endowed with qualities,
possessed of wisdom, gentle, of noble character, learned, devoted to what they have heard, and engaged in proper mental attention.

They were peaceful, self-controlled, thoroughly calmed, speakers who spoke with restraint, possessing a pleasing appearance, virtuous in intention, and avoiders of unwholesome qualities; they were without arrogance, not haughty, not boisterous, and their speech was not scattered; they were established in mindfulness, yet their minds were not fixed in meditative absorption, for they had severed the conduit to existence.

Having extracted the thorns, laid down the burden, crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, and surmounted rebirth, and having recognized that the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, and such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), he serves, frequents, and attends upon them; he pleases them, does not displease them, and delights them. And these...
Having propitiated spiritual friends, they demonstrate, encourage, inspire, and gladden them with discourses on the Dharma; they proclaim that generosity leads to great wealth,
ethical discipline to rebirth in a favorable state, learning to great wisdom, and cultivation to liberation from bondage.

They fully reveal: "This is generosity; this is the ripening of generosity. This is stinginess; this is the ripening of stinginess. This is ethical discipline; this is the ripening of ethical discipline. This is immorality; this..."

This is the maturation of immorality; this is patience, and this is the maturation of patience. This is malice, and this is the maturation of malice. This is vigor, and this is the maturation of vigor. This is laziness, and this is the maturation of laziness.

This is maturation; this is meditation, and this is the maturation of meditation. This is distraction, and this is the maturation of distraction. This is wisdom, and this is the maturation of wisdom. This is lack of wisdom, and this is the maturation of lack of wisdom. This is good conduct of body, and this is the maturation of good conduct of body. This...

This is bodily misconduct; this is the maturation of bodily misconduct. This is verbal good conduct; this is the maturation of verbal good conduct. This is verbal misconduct; this is the maturation of verbal misconduct. This is mental good conduct; this is the maturation of mental good conduct. This is mental misconduct; this is...
This is the maturation of mental misconduct: "This is wholesome; this is unwholesome. This is to be done; this is not to be done.
Having done this, it leads for a long time to what is beneficial, advantageous, pleasant, and security;
but having done that, it leads for a long time to what is harmful, disadvantageous, unpleasant, and insecurity. Thus indeed are those...

Spiritual friends instruct them with a discourse on the Dharma; they encourage, inspire, and gladden them. Recognizing them as fit vessels, he reveals the profound teaching—namely, the discourse on emptiness, the discourse on signlessness, and the discourse on wishlessness.

Discourse on the absence of volitional construction, discourse on the unborn and the unarisen, discourse on selflessness, discourse on selflessness, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a living soul, and the absence of a person,
and discourse on profound dependent origination— namely, that when this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist...
This being, that comes to be; this not being, that does not come to be. This ceasing, that ceases:

namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition...
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, grasping arises;
with grasping as condition, becoming arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.

Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases—namely, from the cessation of ignorance.
With the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.

From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
and from the cessation of birth come the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering; yet,
in the ultimate sense, no phenomenon whatsoever exists here that undergoes either origination or cessation.
Why is that? For all phenomena are dependently originated; they are without an owner, without an agent, and without an experiencer.

They proceed by way of causes and conditions, yet herein no phenomenon whatsoever proceeds, ceases, or revolves. Except for the delusion regarding what has not come to be, there is no designation within the triple world; it is merely the functioning of the afflictions.

[28v3] There is a designation for those who follow karma and follow suffering. For one who examines things as they truly are, there is no perception of what is unreal; no phenomenon whatsoever is the agent of any other phenomenon.
Where an agent is not perceived, there nothing proceeds and nothing ceases. This must be said of him.
Having heard such a profound discourse on the Dharma, he does not waver and does not doubt;
he penetrates the non-attachment of all phenomena and does not cling to form, nor to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He does not cling. He does not cling to the eye, to forms, or to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). He does not cling to the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind, mental objects (*dharma*), or to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). He also has faith that [all these] are empty by nature (*prakṛtiśūnya*).

Friends, a bodhisattva who is thus established in faith regarding all phenomena as being naturally secluded does not fall away from seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, or attending upon the Saṅgha;
wherever he is reborn, there...
He is never separated from the vision of the Buddhas, the hearing of the Dharma, and the service of the Saṅgha;

he is reborn in the presence of the Blessed Buddhas, and having been reborn there, he becomes one who has initiated vigor. Being devoted to the pursuit of wholesome qualities, once his vigor has been initiated, he is free from worldly aims.
He becomes one who has no interest in living as a householder;

he is not possessed by a retinue of wife, sons, daughters, female slaves, male servants, or laborers. Without being quickly led astray by birth, and without sporting with sensual pleasures, he is indeed in the prime of his youth when the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, appear.

Out of faith in the teaching, he goes forth from the home to the homeless life; having gone forth, he obtains spiritual friends, virtuous companions, those who lead him toward what is wholesome, and a virtuous intention. Possessing that virtuous intention, he hears the wholesome teachings and makes practice his essence, rather than being focused on the mere letter.

He becomes endowed with intelligence and exerts vigor in the pursuit of external learning; and he extensively proclaims to others the teachings exactly as they were heard, with a mind free from worldly motives,
not desiring gain, honor, or fame, nor following after his own words for the sake of others.
He teaches the Dharma as it was heard and as it truly exists; he teaches the Dharma to others.

Toward those who listen to the Dharma, he attains great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and toward all sentient beings, he generates great compassion (*karuṇā*). Being thus learned, he remains free from attachment.
He becomes one who has few desires regarding his body and life; he is contented, secluded, easy to support, and easy to maintain;
he delights in remote forest dwellings and examines the teachings exactly as they have been heard. He takes refuge in the meaning and not in the letter, and he becomes a true refuge.

For the world including its gods, humans, and asuras, the purpose of a self that is singular and dissolved does not apply; rather, for the sake of all sentient beings, he seeks the unsurpassed great self, which is this very knowledge of a Buddha. And in this regard, he is supreme in heedfulness (*apramāda*). What, then, is heedlessness? It is the lack of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*); that is to say, with the eye, [perceiving] forms...

Having seen [it], he does not grasp at its signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at its secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Regarding forms (*rūpa*), he understands as they truly are their gratification (*āsvāda*), their danger (*ādīnava*), and the escape from them (*niḥsaraṇa*). The same applies to the ear.

From sound, one does not seize upon signs with the nose regarding odors, nor with the tongue regarding tastes, nor with the body regarding tangibles, nor with the mind regarding mental phenomena (*dharmas*), nor does one seize upon secondary characteristics. One understands, as they truly are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding mental phenomena. This is called heedfulness (*apramāda*). Furthermore:
[29r5] Through heedfulness, there is the taming of one’s own mind, the protection of the minds of others, the removal of delight in the afflictions,
the non-removal of delight in the Dharma, the following of delight in the Dharma,
and the non-occurrence of thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.
It is the non-occurrence of the unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the non-occurrence of misconduct of body, the non-occurrence of misconduct of speech, and the non-occurrence of misconduct of mind;
the non-occurrence of improper mental attention; and the non-occurrence of all evil and unwholesome states.
The absence of activity is called non-laxity. Thus, friends, a bodhisattva who is heedful, applied to appropriate mental attention, and endowed with faith becomes heedful.
O Lord of Guhyakas, be full of faith, always harmonious, devoted to the Dharma, and desirous of the Dharma.

For that person who is faithful, O Lord of Guhyakas, there is no fear of an evil rebirth in the next world; his mind does not incline toward misconduct, and he is praised by the noble ones. Furthermore, O Lord of Guhyakas:

For a person established in the practice of the Dharma, there arises a righteous destiny; they do not lose the vision of the Buddha and are established in the Noble Path. Having attained the state of a Great Being, O Lord of Guhyakas, they [attain] the nature of a Great Being.

[29v1] ...must be fulfilled, namely, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of attaining the knowledge of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Lord of Secrets, a person who wishes to attain happiness should apply themselves to ultimate security and final nirvāṇa. Behold, Lord of Secrets, this assembly’s former...

[29v2] “How does one who has come by means of roots of virtue shine forth there, O Lord of Guhyakas? One should apply oneself to the non-decline of the roots of virtue that are extremely wholesome. And how, O Lord of Guhyakas, do the roots of virtue not decline? For gods and humans, O Lord of Guhyakas, who dwell in heedfulness, the roots of virtue do not decline.”

In that state, there is a decline in lack of joy; there is the guarding of the mind, the relinquishing of sense objects, the avoidance of delight in sensual pleasures, and the cultivation of delight in the Dharma.
There is the non-occurrence of thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty;
the non-occurrence of unwholesome and improper mental attentions; and [the absence of] greed, hatred, and delusion.
The non-occurrence of the depravities of body, speech, and mind, and the non-occurrence of all those factors conducive to decline— this is called heedfulness (*apramāda*). Behold, Lord of Secrets,
faith and heedfulness must be accomplished through corresponding vigor (*vīrya*), by means of which vigor that heedfulness is brought about.

And he will fully accomplish those qualities that inspire faith. Lord of Guhyakas, whoever possesses faith, joy, and vigor must apply themselves to mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-saṃprajanya*), by means of which mindfulness and clear comprehension they do not lose any of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Whoever...
"Lord of Guhyakas, faith, heedfulness, vigor, mindfulness, and discerning awareness— by means of these, one should practice with systematic application.
For, Lord of Guhyakas, a bodhisattva who is engaged in systematic application understands that which exists as 'it exists,' and that which does not exist as 'it does not exist.'"

He understands that "it does not exist. In that regard, what exists and what does not exist? For one who is correctly applied, there is the noble liberation; this is called "what exists. What does not exist therein? For one who is wrongly applied, there is no noble liberation.

This is called "non-existence. Furthermore, there is both action and its maturation. Furthermore, there is that which exists conventionally, yet for which neither action nor maturation exists. Furthermore, there exist conventionally the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

[The rest of the folio is empty] [30r1] For a bodhisattva, all phenomena are his own domain. Just as, Blessed One, the manifestation of all forms is the domain of space, because there is no obstruction to the manifestations of all forms by way of a fixed abode.

Because space has the domain of non-obstruction; even so, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva skilled in means, evil dharmas are his own domain because of their thorough awakening. Just as, Blessed One, the manifestation of all forms is the domain of space because it is unimpaired, whether they be poison trees or medicinal trees.

Whether they be *kaṇṭhaka* trees, flowering trees, fruit trees, or fragrant trees, all of them grow in space; yet space is neither defiled by them nor purified by them. It is not attracted, nor is it repelled. In the same way, Blessed One, it is with the Bodhisattva who is skilled in means and born of wisdom.

All phenomena are one's own domain: those which are the phenomena of ordinary persons, the phenomena of those in training, the phenomena of those beyond training, the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, and those which are the phenomena of the Tathāgata. Why is that? Because all of them must be fully awakened to by him. It is just as if, Blessed One, there were not even a blade of grass or anything at all.

Just as all forest trees become helpful to that fire from which it might flee by providing blazing, heated torches for its ignition; even so, Blessed One, all phenomena are the own-domain of a bodhisattva through the blazing of the torch of wisdom. Just as, Blessed One, the body of a great athlete is not burned by fire...

He is not cut by a weapon, he does not die by poison, and there is no external assault against him. In the same way, Blessed One, the wisdom-knowledge of a bodhisattva cannot be diminished by association with śrāvakas, nor by association with pratyekabuddhas, nor by association with afflictions; and yet again—
Just as he becomes familiar with it, so the Tathāgata or Bodhisattva, devoted to clear vision, refines his wisdom. Just as, O Blessed One,
a water-clearing jewel renders all turbid states transparent, even so...

Blessed One, the jewel of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom clarifies the stain of all afflictions for sentient beings. Blessed One, it is just as if there were a medicine called Vigama; it does not dwell together with poison, yet it neutralizes every kind of venom.

[30r8] ...it acts thus. In the very same way, Blessed One, the cultivation of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva does not dwell together with any affliction, whether it be all afflictions or one's own specific afflictions; and it pacifies the poison of all afflictions. In this very way, Blessed One, the cultivation of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva does not dwell together with any affliction.

And he pacifies the poison of all afflictions in sentient beings. "In this manner, Blessed One, all phenomena are the own-sphere of the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva Śūrabala was teaching thus, O Great King, the minds of eight thousand living beings were set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

[30v2] ...and if, when those [teachings] had arisen, the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) had arisen in two hundred bodhisattvas, then, O Great King, you might think that the bodhisattva named Śūrabala at that time and in that occasion, during the teaching of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vaiśravaṇa, was someone else; but it is not so.
Furthermore, it should not be viewed in this way: it was indeed this very Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas,
who at that time, at that moment, was the bodhisattva named Śūrabala, having donned such an armor of vigor.
"O Great King, he was a true person (satpuruṣa); thus was he one who had attended upon many Buddhas."
The ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Heroic Power. Then, this thought occurred to King Jātaśatru:
"Since Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, has grasped the vajra with his right hand, will it be heavy? Or will it be light, such that this Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas..."

[30v5] ...is called "the bearer of great strength and speed. Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, knowing the thought in King Ajātaśatru’s mind, said this to King Ajātaśatru: "O Great King, this is heavy and it is light. He asked: "For what reason is it heavy?"

"And what is light? He replied: "O Great King, for the sake of subduing sentient beings who are possessed of pride, intoxication, arrogance, and conceit, it is heavy; for those sentient beings who are grave, and for those who are upright, it is light. Then indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, having empowered that region of earth as consisting of vajra, [transformed] that—
He placed the vajra upon the surface of the earth. As soon as it was so placed, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways. Then Vajrapāṇi...
The Lord of the Guhyakas said this to King Ajātaśatru: "O Great King, lift up this vajra from the surface of the earth!
Then King Ajātaśatru, with the force of a great athlete's strength, [lifted] that vajra.

Thinking, "I shall lift it up," he was unable, by the force of all his strength, even to move or shake it by as much as the tip of a hair. Struck with wonder, he joined his palms in reverence and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, with the force of the strength of a great wrestler (*mahānagna*), I can lift with a single hand an elephant clad in armor and mail."
"I am not able to move or shake this very small vajra, let alone [the rest of the folio is empty].
[31r1] This is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Great King of Non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and Noble Right View. He said, "O Blessed One, it is the seclusion of body and mind."
"What is its outflow? He replied, "Great King, the seclusion of body and mind is the outflow of producing meditative absorption and supernormal knowledges.

He asked, "Blessed One, what is the outflow of the Path? He replied, "Great King, the Path is the outflow of the realization of the fruit. He asked, "Blessed One, what is the outflow of resolute conviction? He replied:

“Great King, resolute faith is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) that brings the fulfillment of liberation. He asked: “Blessed One, what is the natural outflow of the appearance of a Buddha? He replied: “Great King, the appearance of a Buddha is the natural outflow of the attainment of all the qualities conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). He asked: “How so, Blessed One, is there the appearance of a Buddha? He replied:

"Just as, Great King, is the arising of the thought of awakening. He asked: "How, Blessed One, is there the arising of the thought of awakening? He replied: "Just as, Great King, is the arising of great compassion. He asked: "Whose, Blessed One, is the arising of a Buddha? He replied: "Whose, Great King, is the arising of faith. He asked: "Whose, Blessed One..."

[The King asked: "What is the arising of the thought of awakening? He replied: "It is that, O Great King, for which there is the arising of the thought of awakening. [The King asked: "Whose, Blessed One, is the arising of the thought of awakening? He replied: "It is that, O Great King, whose resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is unshakable.
[The King asked: "Whose, Blessed One, is the resolute intention unshakable? He replied: "It is that, O Great King, for whom there is the arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
He asked: "Blessed One, how is the arising of great compassion? He replied: "Great King, it is like the arising of non-abandonment toward sentient beings.
He asked: "Blessed One, how are sentient beings not abandoned?"

[They] come to be. He said: "When, Great King, one has relinquished one's own happiness. He asked: "But how, Blessed One, is one's own happiness relinquished? He replied: "Great King, for one who has not relinquished the Three Jewels. He asked: "Whose, Blessed One, are the Three Jewels?"

[They have been] relinquished. He said: "Great King, for one by whom all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been relinquished, the Three Jewels (*triratna*) have not been relinquished. Then King Ajātaśatru said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One!
It is wonderful, Sugata! How well-spoken is the entrance of the Tathāgata!"

The Dharma and Vinaya have been realized; the training of the Tathāgata has been well-proclaimed; the Dharma-teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is entirely consistent with reality; there is no loss of cause and fruit; there is the departure from both annihilationism and eternalism;
there is the instruction on entering into the performance of actions; and there is the non-confusion of the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious.

“O Blessed One, what person who is devoted to this very sublime and excellent teaching—characterized by non-deception and the absence of destruction—would reject, obstruct, or oppose it? It is only those who have not planted roots of merit and are possessed by evil friends; we ourselves, O Blessed One, would not do so.”

We must be ungrateful toward our former roots of merit and toward the Tathāgata; we are not able to repay him even with our own flesh and blood, by whose power we have been turned away from all afflictions.
And likewise, O Blessed One, toward Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, who has long been our spiritual friend.

[31v3] We are unable to repay him, by whose power we have dispelled this great and unwholesome remorse and attained a great illumination of the Dharma. Well-spoken indeed are these words of the Blessed One: "This entire holy life consists in this, namely, the possession of a virtuous friend. Thus ends the section concerning Ajātaśatru.

The tenth chapter, named "The Transformation. Then the bodhisattva Śāntamati said this to Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas: "Lord of the Guhyakas, when the Blessed One creates an emanation, do you also at that time create an emanation? Vajrapāṇi replied:

This Blessed One is present before me; he is my witness: if, noble son, the Tathāgata were to emanate as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, just as many emanations of mine would follow after them, assuming various forms and performing various miraculous displays. This, noble son, is the former purification...

This is the natural outflow of a perfected intention. Then the Bodhisattva Śāntamati said this to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas: "O Lord of Guhyakas, entreat the Tathāgata so that this Dharma-discourse may circulate in the final age, during the last five hundred years."
And it shall become widespread;
it shall come into the hands of those virtuous persons who uphold the true Dharma. The Lord of the Guhyakas said:
"Noble sons, this Dharma-discourse has been empowered by all the Buddhas. For what reason? Because of the syllables by which..."
This Dharma-discourse has indicated those syllables which are not real, yet they do not perish nor do they disappear;
and the meaning expressed by those syllables—that meaning also cannot be made to disappear.
Noble son, the True Dharma of the Tathāgata does not disappear. Why is that? Because there is no such thing as an arising, and...

It does not arise, nor does it cease. With this in mind, the Blessed One said: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the suchness of phenomena (dharma-yathāvattā) remain fixed. And thus, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is not contradicted.

That which is not in contradiction with dependent origination is the true Dharma; and that which is the true Dharma is always present and has not disappeared. Therefore, it is called the "True Dharma."
[32r2] Śāntamati said: "Lord of Guhyakas, those who arm themselves for the sake of upholding the true Dharma—where do they arm themselves? He replied:

"Those who arm themselves for the sake of upholding the true Dharma arm themselves for the sake of non-contradiction with all phenomena. Why is that? For this very thing is the true Dharma: that which [is non-contradictory] with all phenomena..."

[There is] no contradiction. He asked: "How does there come to be a contradiction regarding the Dharma? He replied: "A contradiction regarding the Dharma arises from a contradiction regarding the syllables; however, the Dharma itself is never contradicted. In that regard, those who are not in contradiction are the upholders of the True Dharma. He asked: "O Lord of the Guhyakas, could there be a way in which all..."
He who is opposed to the world upholds the true Dharma. He said: "For what reason would that be so?

Noble son, the world is attached to views, whereas he is a proponent of emptiness; therefore, he is opposed to the entire world. The world speaks of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self, whereas he speaks of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self."

He is a proponent of non-self; therefore, he is in opposition to the whole world. The world flows with the current, while he flows against the current; therefore, he is in opposition to the whole world. The world values the present life, while he values the future life; therefore, he is in opposition to the whole world. The world is attached to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

And he teaches the Dharma for the sake of non-attachment to all phenomena; therefore, he is at variance with the entire world. By this method, noble son, he who is at variance with the entire world upholds the true Dharma. He asked:
"O Lord of Guhyakas, do you uphold the true Dharma? He replied: "I uphold it."

“I do not grasp, noble son, at a self, nor do I grasp at a sentient being, nor at phenomena. He asked: ‘How do I grasp? [I replied: ‘By way of the solitude of the self, the solitude of sentient beings, and the solitude of phenomena;
by way of the non-solitude of self, sentient beings, and phenomena; and by way of the non-solitude of the past, future, and present.’”

[32r8] By way of being secluded from the past, future, and present time-epochs; by way of being secluded from the Buddha and not being non-secluded from the Buddha; by way of being secluded from the field and not being non-secluded from the field; by way of being secluded from phenomena and not being non-secluded from phenomena—this very following after phenomena is the grasping of the true Dharma. Then, indeed, the Lord...
[32v1] To Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, he gave his approval, saying: "Excellent, excellent, O noble being!

This is the upholding of the true Dharma. Moreover, O lord of the Guhyakas, that upholding of the true Dharma is the non-grasping and non-clinging to all phenomena; it is the [non-apprehension of] the conceptual proliferations regarding the signs of sentient beings."

Grasping is the manifestation of all conceptualizations—whether they are non-conceptual or free from conceptualization. Furthermore, at that time, a son of the gods named Bhadrarāja, having assembled in that assembly, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“O Blessed One, the word of the Buddha is tranquility; for one who is tranquil, O Blessed One...”
[32v3] Where is that which is the word of the Buddha? For one who is stilled, that is the word of the Buddha.

In this regard, Blessed One, those who see all objective supports as stilled are themselves stilled; they will not ignite further, they do not blaze, and they do not cause others to blaze. Those who are calm, thoroughly pacified, and stilled—those are they.

They uphold the true Dharma of the Tathāgata, and they uphold it in such a way that all phenomena are not upheld. As that son of the gods was thus instructing, the minds of one thousand monks were liberated, and the Dharma-eye of one thousand sons of the gods was purified. Then Śānta—

The Bodhisattva Mati said this to the divine son Bhadrarāja: "Divine son, whose is this eloquence? He replied: "It is the eloquence of one for whom all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) have been abandoned, who has departed from the paths of speech, who is not attached to that which is ineffable and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). He said: "Eloquence..."
[32v6] “How, O son of the gods, does that discourse arise? He replied: “By way of eloquence and by way of non-eloquence.

Why is that? ‘Non-eloquence’ is a statement that lacks connection; ‘non-eloquence’ is the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Furthermore, noble son, as for what you have said: ‘Ka...’”

This is his inspired eloquence: he for whom consciousness does not proceed toward either body or communication, and whose consciousness is not established even in self-communication; this is his inspired eloquence, he for whom [consciousness does not proceed] toward an objective referent (*ālambana*).
Mental representation has no objective support, and they abide in the state of unobstructed dharmatā.

This is the eloquence of one whose knowledge does not operate with respect to any phenomena, and for whom no phenomenon whatsoever is cognized by means of knowledge; this is the eloquence of one who, being established, crosses the flood without grasping.
This is his inspired eloquence: that which has arisen from non-arising will pass into nirvāṇa through non-cessation.
This is his inspired eloquence. Then the bodhisattva Śāntati said this to the Blessed One:
"It is marvelous, Blessed One, the inspired eloquence of this divine son Bhadrarāja. The Blessed One said: "This..."
Noble son, the divine son Bhadrarāja has come here from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya,

from the world-system Abhirati, in order to hear this Dharma discourse, the secret of the Tathāgatas, the teaching of Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas. This, noble son, is the divine son Bhadrarāja.

There is a dhāraṇī called "Entry into the Forms of Dharmas. One who has obtained it could, for a hundred thousand aeons, explain it with unimpeded eloquence according to their desire, yet their eloquence would never come to an end. Śāntamati said: "Blessed One, what is that dhāraṇī called 'Entry into the Forms of Dharmas'?"

The Blessed One said: "Noble son, the entry into the aspects of phenomena (dharmākāra) is the knowledge that enters into syllables by means of syllables. Noble son, 'aspect' (ākāra) is the entry into all phenomena;
all phenomena have aspects as their gateway, they are produced from aspects, and they culminate in aspects. In every instance of vocal action, aspect is the activity."
It performs the aspect, yet it neither knows nor discerns;

the entry into the aspects of all phenomena is called the *dhāraṇī* named "Entry into the Aspects of Phenomena. Noble son, as for this entry, not even a single phenomenon has entered there, nor has it departed; noble son, those...
Syllables do not come from anywhere and enter into the inner chamber; nor do those syllables remain within the inner chamber; nor do those syllables depart toward any direction after emerging;
nor do those syllables mutually ignite one another; nor are those syllables [identical to] "Dharma."

Or they conceive of them as non-dharma. Furthermore, those syllables—whether spoken or unspoken—neither diminish nor increase; nor have those syllables been produced or extinguished by anyone, nor have those syllables been created or destroyed by anyone, just as it is.
Noble son, the calculation of syllables is just like the calculation of the mind;

as is the calculation of the mind, so is the calculation of all phenomena; as is the calculation of all phenomena, so is non-calculation. For what reason? Because non-calculation does not enter into the calculation of phenomena.

The reckoning of phenomena (*dharmagaṇanā*). Just as a phenomenon does not undergo reckoning, such is the entry into its aspect (*ākārānupraveśa*). From the very beginning it is born (or rather, unborn); this entry is the entry into non-arising (*anutpādapraveśa*).
That which is neither born nor arisen has no entry whatsoever. Thus, this non-entry is the true entry. And that which...
Noble son, having entered this calculation, it is impossible for anyone to interrupt his eloquence.

Why is that? Because it is uninterrupted; therefore, it conforms to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and is inexhaustible; therefore, it conforms to the nature of phenomena. In whatever way he teaches the Dharma, in that very way those phenomena are expressed and become manifest.
He enters into the manifestation of sentient beings by means of this very form, in order to enter into the aspects of the Dharma.

[Page 48, 58 [33v3]] Thus, by entering into the modes of beings, he teaches the Dharma according to their inclinations. Śāntamati, the bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī becomes stainless, his mind is purified, and he is pure in his resolute intention.
He becomes one who acts with application; he becomes one who has risen up through his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*);

he becomes well-established in practice; he becomes one who has risen up through wisdom (*prajñā*); he becomes firm in fulfilling his vow; he becomes unbreakable by the Māras; and he becomes unsurpassed by the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*).

He becomes difficult for the afflictions to overcome; he becomes uncrushable by adversaries; he becomes strong in body; he becomes undaunted in mind; he becomes inexhaustible in eloquence; he becomes infinite in explanations; he becomes boundless in definitions; he becomes free from doubt through knowledge; he is difficult to fathom...

He becomes profound through his intelligence; he becomes deep in the teachings of the truth; he becomes like the ocean in his learning; he becomes like Mount Meru in his meditative concentration; he becomes like a lion in the assemblies;
he becomes like a lotus amidst worldly conditions; and he becomes like the earth in being the sustenance for all sentient beings.

He becomes like water by dispelling the thirst of the afflictions; he becomes like fire by bringing all sentient beings to maturity; he becomes like the moon by having a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
and he becomes like the sun by dispelling the darkness of the afflictions; he becomes like a hero.
By way of destroying the enemies that are the afflictions, he is like a nāga through having a well-tamed mind; he is like a cloud by thundering the Dharma; he is like rain by pouring down the Dharma;
he is like a physician by pacifying the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings; he is like a king.
By not exercising dominion over the kingdom of Dharma, he becomes equal to a world-protector (*lokapāla*); by protecting the worldly dharma, he becomes equal to Śakra;

as a supervisor of gods and humans, he becomes equal to Brahmā; having attained offspring through mastery over his own mind, he becomes like a bird due to his homeless wandering; he becomes like a deer or a monkey.

Trembling with fear of social entanglement, he becomes like a mother to all sentient beings by exhausting all their misdeeds; he becomes like a father by teaching them all the arts and crafts; he becomes like Vaiśravaṇa by bestowing the jewels of all dharmas. He is adorned with merits and embellished with the primary marks.

He becomes radiant with the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*); he becomes beautiful to behold; he becomes a source of attraction for the world by his very appearance. He does not become poor, being endowed with the seven riches; he is embraced by the Buddhas; and he becomes worthy of praise.

Regarding consciousnesses: he becomes one who cannot be refuted by any scholars; he is well-guarded by the gods and well-sustained by the *nāgas* and *yakṣas*; he becomes a master in the teaching of the Dharma and possesses sovereign power over the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

They will have served for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons; they will have performed their preparatory practices and planted excellent roots of merit in this Mahāyāna.
